motivation: In 1979 Tajima (with the late J. M. Dawson) proposed that an intense laser pulse can drive a plasma wake whose fields exceed those of conventional radio-frequency accelerators by three orders of magnitude. Malka and Leemans led the experiments that turned this idea into a working accelerator. Malka's team produced quasi-monoenergetic electron beams from millimetre-scale plasmas, and Leemans' team used guided, channel-based schemes to reach GeV and later multi-GeV energies over centimetres. Laser-plasma accelerators now drive compact femtosecond X-ray and gamma-ray sources and early free-electron-laser demonstrations. They have also opened experimental strong-field QED: collisions of wakefield beams with intense lasers have shown radiation reaction and quantum effects in the emission of radiation. This work created a new field that joins plasma physics, laser science and fundamental electrodynamics, and it offers a route to much smaller accelerators.
